title: Why sovereign: owning every layer
summary: Drake builds his own AI on hardware he owns, with every layer from the kernel up open to read, rebuild and change. Sovereign Intelligence (SI), built on AienOS, is the package; aienux is the kernel; AienOS-nv is the OS's home. He names his boundary plainly: the GB10 silicon and NVIDIA's signed firmware are not his, and SI alpha still runs on the Spark's Linux. I can show you how to check what a binary needs below it: an Omega program reads ELF headers and proves omc's output needs no loader and no libc.
goal: Understand what a sovereign stack is, where SI sits in it, and check that an omc-built program depends on nothing but the kernel.
key_steps: Read the ten-layer stack map in docs/STACK.md and note each layer's evidence level
Name the boundary you do not own (silicon, signed firmware, today's kernel driver)
Compile elfinfo.om with the pinned omc and run it on omc and on itself
Run it on /bin/sh as a negative control and see the loader it needs
Give every layer you still depend on its own evidence level

example.code:
note elfinfo: read a 64-bit little-endian ELF file on stdin and say whether it needs a loader
note PT_INTERP (3) names a dynamic loader and PT_DYNAMIC (2) lists shared libraries; a file with neither
note runs on the kernel alone. exit 0 static, 1 needs a loader or libraries, 3 not an ELF64 LE file, 4 too big
text telf "elf64 little-endian\n"
text ttype "type "
text tmach "machine "
text tph "program headers "
text tload "PT_LOAD "
text tdyn "PT_DYNAMIC "
text tint "PT_INTERP "
text vstat "verdict STATIC: no loader, no shared libraries, only kernel system calls below it\n"
text vdyn "verdict DYNAMIC: needs a loader and shared libraries before its first instruction\n"
text vnot "verdict NOT_ELF64\n"
text vbig "verdict REFUSED input too big\n"
text nl "\n"
global ph ulong 4
fn rd16 o ulong to ulong
ret or ulong get inb o shl ulong get inb add o 1 8
end
fn rd32 o ulong to ulong
ret or rd16 o shl rd16 add o 2 16
end
fn rd64 o ulong to ulong
ret or rd32 o shl rd32 add o 4 32
end
fn kv t view uchar * v ulong to void
ot t
on v
ot nl
end
fn isel n ulong to bool
note magic 127 E L F, class 2 (64-bit), data 1 (little-endian)
if lt n 64
ret false
end
if ne get inb 0 127
ret false
end
if ne get inb 1 69
ret false
end
if ne get inb 2 76
ret false
end
if ne get inb 3 70
ret false
end
if ne get inb 4 2
ret false
end
if ne get inb 5 1
ret false
end
ret true
end
fn scan n ulong to bool
note count segment types; false when the header table is not inside the file
off = rd64 32
esz = rd16 54
cnt = rd16 56
if gt off n
ret false
end
if gt mul esz cnt sub n off
ret false
end
if lt esz 4
ret false
end
for i ulong cnt
t = rd32 add off mul i esz
if lt t 4
put ph t add get ph t 1
end
end
ret true
end
fn main to int
r = rdall
if lt r 0
ret 4
end
if eq get st 2 1
ot vbig
f = flush
ret 4
end
n = ulong r
ok = isel n
if ok
ok = scan n
end
if not ok
ot vnot
f = flush
ret 3
end
ot telf
kv ttype rd16 16
kv tmach rd16 18
kv tph rd16 56
kv tload get ph 1
kv tdyn get ph 2
kv tint get ph 3
v = int 0
if gt add get ph 2 get ph 3 0
v = 1
ot vdyn
else
ot vstat
end
f = flush
ret v
end

common_mistake: Calling something independent because one library was removed. Check what is really loaded (PT_INTERP, PT_DYNAMIC, /proc/PID/maps) and list the layers you still rely on. Also keep the names straight: SI is the package, AienOS the operating system, Aienux the kernel.

evidence_note: The ELF check ran on a Linux arm64 host with the pinned omc, with two negative controls. It shows the binaries need no loader or shared library; it does not show anything about the kernel or GPU driver below them. Nothing in the stack is hardware QUALIFIED; Aienux has not booted on the Spark.
